title: What manner of love (1 John 3:1–3)
hook: see what love: that we should be called children of God

segments.voice: Yesterday: little children, the writer's pet name, and lines written from what's already true. Your line was the world passeth away.

Somewhere in a lot of families there's a box: crayon drawings, a first shoe, a report card, a lock of hair. Plenty of people only find it as adults, clearing out a closet, and it stops them cold: someone kept all of this, because it was mine. A love they never saw, kept the whole time. Today's passage is three verses long, and it begins with that kind of surprise. The writer has been talking about light and darkness, sin and commandments. Then he stops, as if overcome, and says: look.

In the King James Bible: "Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God." Behold: look at this. What manner of love: the Greek phrase carries surprise, something like, what kind of love is this? Bestowed is a gift word. Not earned. Given. And the gift is a name: called children of God. A detail from the manuscripts: the oldest Greek manuscripts add three more words, and so we are. Called children of God, and so we are. The manuscripts behind the King James didn't have them, and modern translations usually put them back. It's as if the writer worried someone would think called was only a title. It's what you are. Then why the world doesn't always see it: "therefore the world knoweth us not, because it knew him not." If people missed who Jesus was, they'll miss his children too. Then the future, and what he admits he doesn't know: "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be." Already, but not yet finished. What he does know is that when he appears, "we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is." And the last verse says hope like that changes how you live now: whoever has this hope purifies himself.
screen: `BEHOLD: WHAT KIND OF LOVE IS THIS?`
`NOW, BUT NOT YET WHAT WE SHALL BE.`
`WE SHALL SEE HIM AS HE IS.`

segments.voice: Notice the names you call yourself in a hard moment, failure, too much, not enough, without arguing with them. Then set beside them the name the letter uses, children of God, with your own name in front of it if you pray, or a plainer one if that phrase isn't yours: I am loved. Rest there, and just look.
Bestowed. First John's gift word, not earned, but given: the Father's love that lets us be called children of God, and so we are.
Your line: children of god. Called, and so we are. That's day six hundred eighty-five.

screen: `DAY 685 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IN DEED AND IN TRUTH.`

howItsDone: Many Christians read 1 John 3:1–2 at baptisms and on All Saints' Day, and the line about seeing God as he is shapes Christian hope in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teaching alike.

fork.reveal: the oldest manuscripts read, called children of God, and so we are. not only a name: a fact.

original.note: Greek: what kind of, what sort of, often with a note of wonder. the word behind 'what manner of'.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet verse about God loving everyone.
what it means: a gift of belonging so surprising the writer says 'look', already true now, with more not yet seen.
what a scholar hears: 'and so we are' (kai esmen) is in the oldest manuscripts but missing from the KJV's Greek text; and potapēn, a word of wonder.

chat.says: Is 'children of God' just a nice title in First John, or something more?
options: More: the oldest manuscripts add 'and so we are.' Called God's children, and truly so, as a gift.
Just a title: the writer says it only becomes true once we see him as he is.
Something you earn: the love is bestowed on those who've kept every commandment.
chat.meaning: Bestowed means given, not earned. The oldest manuscripts add 'and so we are': not only a title, but what we are.

bestowed.meaning: given as a gift, not earned

manuscripts.meaning: handwritten copies of the Bible's text

notes: καὶ ἐσμέν ('and so we are') in 3:1 is in the major early manuscripts (e.g. Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus) and absent from the Textus Receptus behind the KJV. Confirm.
KJV 'sons of God' (Greek τέκνα, children); the carry 'children of god' follows the Greek. Confirm.
ποταπός as 'of what sort', with a note of wonder; the older derivation 'from what country' is uncertain and is not used.
Use of 1 John 3:1–3 on All Saints' Day (it is a reading in several lectionaries) and at baptisms: confirm.
The carry's lowercase 'god' follows the index exactly; the spoken voice says it naturally.

Audit (second sample): hook used an adoption hearing, a belonging image that repeats day 684's family pet names and fits Paul's adoption language better than First John's (which speaks of being born of God); now a kept box of childhood things. Cut stock lines ('a detail scholars love', 'Christians across traditions have treasured this line'). Practice and carry no longer tell the listener to call themselves a child of God; it is offered 'if you pray', with a plain alternative.
